speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today's Ottawa Citizen tells us that 9,962 companies have gone bankrupt in the first 11 months of this year, leaving behind them some $2.1 billion in debt. This represents an increase of 35.4 per cent over the same period last year, and 411 per cent over the 2,420 recorded during the height of the 1930s' depression.
The Party opposite has clung to power for 15 years by claiming to be able to unite our country. While its members efforts in every other regard have been utter failures-even to the point of being counter-productive-honesty compels us to acknowledge the unity they have forced upon all of us by their economic policies. Therefore I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Corbett):
That this House congratulate the Government for at last fulfilling, at least in part, its pledge to unify the country-even if that unifying force is despair-and urges it to quit while it is at least this far ahead.

subsubtopic: IDENTIFICATION OF TRUCKS CARRYING DANGEROUS CARGO
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today on an issue vital to the safety of Canadians. Last month a tanker truck carrying an explosive liquid rolled over on the Queen Elizabeth Way. Firefighters were unaware of the contents of the trunk and exposed themselves to an unknown danger. Later the Transportation Minister for the Ontario Government, when asked why there were no laws to force truckers carrying dangerous goods to label their vehicles for easy
identification of their contents, told the press that he could not do so until federal regulations are in place.
Given that the Minister has been pressing the federal Government for five years on this matter and that the wellbeing of Canadian citizens is at stake, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges):
That the Government immediately draft legislation requiring trucks to carry signs identifying dangerous cargo with a view to preventing serious accidents of this nature in the future.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the continuing denial of human rights in many parts of the world and the continuing need to urge all Governments to adhere to the substance as well as the spirit of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) and the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald):
That this House note that today, December 10, 1982, is the thirty-fourth anniversary of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights, express its appreciation of and support for the important work being done by the United Nations Human Rights Commission, Amnesty International, and the Helsinki monitoring groups, and urge all nations to adhere to the spirit and the substance of the United Nations Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

As I said before, Madam Speaker, I hope that all private organizations in Canada with a deep commitment to human rights will take appropriate action in order to meet the objectives set forth in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
As Secretary of State, I shall also have an opportunity to report to this House on the manner in which Canada has met its commitments to two extremely important international conventions one on eliminating racial discrimination, and this report will be tabled at the end of this year, and the other on eliminating discrimination against women, with a report to be tabled at the beginning of 1983. Madam Speaker, this thirty-fourth anniversary of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a day to which we all want to pay respect, as indeed the world community has done for 34 years in its efforts to enhance and respect human rights.
We know, nevertheless, that human rights have been violated time and time again throughout the world. So often we just use this occasion to pay lip service to a significant day,
but one of the steps that we, as Canadian Parliamentarians, can take is to implement the recommendation that has been made to this House to establish a Parliamentary Association on Human Rights. In that way, as legislators in this Chamber we can give continuing and consistent support wherever human rights violations take place, whether they be in our own country or in any part of the world. We have an opportunity to set up an association and do something more than just pay lip service to this Universal Declaration of Human Rights once a year.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER INVOLVING SMALL BUSINESSES-EFFECT OF BUDGET
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Finance. 1 am sure he is aware of the announcement of the bankruptcy figures for November of this year, which are up 35 per cent over the same period last year, and for the period to date this year 38,000 bankruptcies have been declared. Since almost all of these bankruptcies relate to small businesses, could the Minister explain why the Government has persisted in retaining so many parts of the disastrous November budget which hurt small business so badly? 1 am referring to such things as the 12.5 per cent dividend tax, the effective removal of the deferred profit sharing plans, the loss of the cumulative dividend account, the reduction of capital cost allowances, much tighter treatment of the reserve provisions of capital gains, and others besides those.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of State (Finance)):
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER INVOLVING SMALL BUSINESSES-EFFECT OF BUDGET
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of Finance, in his statement to the House on October 28, indicated that the Government was concerned about the plight of the small business sector. In response to that, a number of changes have been made to the proposals in the November, 1981, budget. For example, an item talked about by the Hon. Member, that is the distribution tax on dividends and its supposed retroactivity, has been eliminated and the section simplified. A number of steps have been taken by the Minister. There are a number of provisions in the Bill placed before the House which have been well received by the business community, for example, the extension of the Small Business Bond until the end of 1983.
Of course it is the wish of the Minister, and I am sure of the Hon. Member who asked the question, that these provisions be dealt with quickly by the House so that they can be put into force. Perhaps there are some with which the Hon. Member does not agree but, nevertheless, they would bring certainty to the business community. We would urge quick consideration of those provisions.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN NUMBER INVOLVING SMALL BUSINESSES-EFFECT OF BUDGET

1 should remind the Minister that the 12.5 per cent dividend tax is still there. If he says that this is well received by the business community, as always he is totally out of touch with what is going on with small business people in the country.
The announcement this morning represents 38,000 broken dreams. It also represents 38,000 people and their families who have had their nest eggs for the future destroyed. Also it means that many jobs related to those businesses have been lost.

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT INTRODUCE NATIONAL PROGRAM OF RECOVERY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. During the past seven sitting days of the House Members of the New Democratic Party have raised no fewer than 23 specific sections in the unemployment crisis in this country as areas to make constructive proposals to the Government in order to create jobs. On the one hand the Government's response has been arrogant indifference and, on the other hand, simply to dismiss the proposals out of hand. It has not accepted one idea. In the face of the continuing massive lay-offs that are occurring all over the country, will the Government now come to its senses, accept its social responsibility, and announce that it will bring in a national program of recovery before Christmas?

Old Age Security Act (No. 2)

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, November 30, consideration of the motion of Miss Begin that Bill C-131, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act (No. 2), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are debating Bill C-131 today. It is a Bill to reduce old age pensions by allowing for indexing of only 6 per cent for Old Age Security this year and 5 per cent next year; hardly the rate of inflation which is well over 10 per cent. Even the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) stated her agreement at the National Pension Conference when she said:
Pensions which are not protected against inflation naturally tend to dwindle over the years. People who thought they had purchased protection for the rest of their lives find they have more serious financial problems the older they become.
With inflation as it is, I am shocked that the Government can even consider restraining the already limited income of senior citizens and further adding to their financial burdens.
It would seem to me that our older population is not being given the consideration they have earned. Due to the fact that we had 2,360,975 senior citizens living in Canada in 1981 and that this number is increasing at the rate of 3 per cent per year, I feel it necessary that action be taken immediately to ensure that the voices of our senior citizens are heard. It is important that they be easily able to inform us of their thoughts and concerns, as well as share with us their collective experience and judgment, which might better enable us to deal more effectively with their problems.
Therefore, I am proposing that a Senior Citizens' parliament be formed, similar to that of the very successful Canadian Youth Parliament and based upon the same idea as the organization established in Florida, namely the Silver-Haired Legislature. A number of articles have been written in the Manitoba "Seniors Journal" by Mr. H. W. Brown of Winnipeg on this very subject.
The State of Florida Silver-Haired Legislature was commenced some years ago, and at least ten other States are in the organizing stage of similar legislatures. The successful attempt to convince various groups of the need for such an organization was brought forward by the identification of what was perceived to be important and necessary concerns for the over-all and ultimate well-being of older adults. Promotion, public information and the mass media brought to the public interest the potential of such a seniors' lobby. Funded through the Older Americans Act, the first Silver-Haired Legislature was organized and co-ordinated by the Department of Health and Rehabilitative Services, Office of Aging and Adult Services, and co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters and Florida
State University. Responsibility for monitoring and administering the over-all operation of this legislature lies within the structure of the State Office of Aging and Adult Services. Personnel of the various area and local programs were convinced of the value of the Silver-Haired Legislature and trained to organize the necessary tasks for electing persons to the legislature.
The following goals reflect the intent of implementing the Silver-Haired Legislature:
(a)	To provide an educational opportunity for the elderly to learn through participation in legislative activities.
(b)	To increase the level of participation and involvement of retired professionals that may have no prior or continuing contact with older adult programs.
(c)	To develop a collective awareness among older persons with regard to needs, issues and policies that are of concern to themselves and their age cohorts.
(d)	To stimulate community organization involvement with groups of older adults, and
(e)	To provide a stronger base for influencing policy which reflects the self-perceived needs of the older population.
We will all be part of the Silver-Haired Legislature sooner or later. Not all of us; as I look around the Chamber I see that some still have a bit of brown hair.

speechtext: You missed the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon).

speechtext: Why have I been left out of this legislation?

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Because of the increasing number of senior citizens in Canada, we are certainly not at a loss for people to become involved in such a plan. For example, the National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation is comprised of more than 400,000 members. In my own riding alone, we have the St. Andrews Over 60 Group, the 1600 Recreation Club, the Boulton Bay Seniors Association, the Sturgeon Creekers Over 60 Club, the Hamilton House Recreation Club, the Hendon Avenue Residents Tenants Society, and the Carefree Curling and Recreation Association. They are only a few of the many seniors' groups which could become active in such a mini-parliament.
One group which comes to mind is the Rail Pensioners organization. There has never been a group in Canada which has been treated so shabbily by successive Liberal Governments; they have been given the runaround for years. The group could certainly become part of a senior citizens' parliament to explain how they have been shabbily treated and have received a mere pittance each year in terms of increases in their pensions.
Every Senior citizens' organization across Canada could elect a representative who would meet as often as necessary with other elected Seniors under one umbrella. They could discuss the obstacles being encountered by the older population and their solutions and then collectively make representation to the tederal Government. This parliament would not only have the power of recommendation but would undoubtedly
December 10, 1982

tend to influence public opinion, as well as hopefully make the Government more aware of its concerns, problems and needs which are now, particularly today, being so carelessly overlooked.
Legislative successes in the State of Florida are indicative of the effectiveness of a self-advocacy model. Furthermore, this approach provides an opportunity for the implementation and expansion of the political input of the elderly. The presence of a potential age-related backlash could be offset by an awareness of community issues which include those issues confronting older adults.
An immediate example would be the issue which we are discussing now, that of Bill C-131. Certainly the increased visibility of the issues facing the older adult population specifically can serve to reduce the misconceptions of the community at large which might result in a hesitancy to support policies affecting the elderly.
In Florida the successes of the Silver-Haired Legislature delegates include the funding of bills for community care for the elderly and recommended the spending of $11.8 million which was increased by the Legislature to $13.2 million. A Silver-Haired Legislature bill mandating Medicaid payments for eye glasses, hearing aids and dentures recommended $3 million, and this was raised to $5 million by the Legislature. A Silver-Haired Legislature in Canada could recommend spending authority, but that would probably be the extent of it. With the urging of the SHL, the Legislature allocated $2.5 million to help with transportation for the elderly and handicapped. Hospital cost containment was taken up by the regular Legislature, and a special committee on aging was created. A recommendation that seniors be nominated to advisory boards resulted in seniors being appointed to at least five State-wide boards.
It is fairly evident that the Florida experiment has been highly valuable to seniors, the general public, advisory boards and the State Legislature. Therefore, I would ask that the Government take into consideration my proposal, as I am sure it could be as successful here in Canada and invaluable when we in the House of Commons debate subjects such as Bill C-131, which is only one issue, if passed, that will drastically affect the lives of Canadian senior citizens.
We have just received this document from the Government which is entitled "Better Pensions for Canadians". In the Foreword we find these words:
Many Canadians have expressed concern over the adequacy and fairness of the retirement income system. In response to these concerns, the Government of Canada is putting forward for discussion and debate a number of proposals for reform. These proposals will be referred to a Parliamentary Committee, where all interested parties and the public at large will have the opportunity to express their views.
The establishment of a senior citizens' parliament might be the way to do this. These comments continue:
Consultations must be as broad and effective as possible in the revision and improvement of Government policies.

That, of course, would fall in line with the formation of a senior citizens' parliament which would meet, say, on an annual basis or twice a year to discuss problems and make presentations to the Government.
It has always been Progressive Conservative policy to maintain the quality of life on retirement, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, so that we can spend time studying the recent report "Better Pensions for Canadians" before we start cutting any more old age pensions, I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker):

hence".
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this should receive the approval of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I do not frequently speak on this subject in this House because my friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who has been here for almost 40 years, has made hundreds, if not thousands, of speeches and asked questions about old age pensions. To a large extent I felt I could leave the subject to him, but because of the fact that he has not been well and is not able to participate in this debate today, 1 thought I would try to do the best I could to put the case against the proposals in this Bill as he would have done.
It is interesting and somewhat significant that we are debating and will vote on this Bill today, a day after the Government, through the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), finally, and very belatedly, tabled its green paper on pension reform. In the last two years there have been 15 major studies on pension reform. These have been done by groups appointed by the federal Government, by some provincial Governments, by trade unions and by business. Yet here we are debating a Bill that will limit the increases old age pensioners will get. These increases will be limited to 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year. Yet the green paper makes it very clear, as does the Minister, that there is much wrong with the pension system as we have it, and that so many people are dealt with in a miserly niggardly way.
In the Minister's press release of yesterday when she tabled the green paper, she said, in part:
Reform of the pension system is important because there are serious deficiencies relating to coverage, inflation protection, portability and the treatment of women. As a result, many Canadians face a significant decline in living standards on retirement due to inadequate pension incomes.
Having said that yesterday, the Minister today brings forward a Bill which will reduce the protection which our old age pensioners had against the increased cost of living.

December 10, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
There are blatant contradictions between the public declarations which this Minister has made over the years and her actions in the House sponsoring what we consider to be a repugnant and despicable piece of legislation. We condemn that.
While the Minister bemoans the lack of inflation protection and said that "women suffer most from deficiencies in the current pension system", she sponsors this Bill which cuts inflation protection and the already meagre stipends that over
100.000	elderly Canadians, the majority of them women, exist on. While piously declaring herself for pension reform, the Minister of National Health and Welfare puts before us legislation to erode a system which she herself has stated again and again is inadequate.
The Government argues that any loss in Old Age Security will be made up by an adjustment in the Guaranteed Income Supplement. If an individual receives $6,123 or more in outside income-perhaps in savings-this individual is disqualified from receiving GIS. The individual would receive $3,058 per annum from OAS, and his or her outside income, making a total as low as $9,200 a year. What these individuals are receiving from the Minister is a kick in the teeth, not pension reform.
The National Council on Welfare estimates that over
100.000	of Canada's elderly citizens "fall through the cracks this way". In cities such as Toronto, they would exist at a level 37 per cent below the officially recognized poverty line. In rural areas Canada's elderly citizens exist at a level 15 per cent below the officially recognized poverty line.
The United Church of Canada commissioned a report recently entitled "Income Security". We find in this report the following:
It would seem that increases in the OAS, the GIS, and provincial supplements may have been sufficient to move many older couples from the "poor" to the "near-poor" category, but leaving a large number of single elderly people below the poverty line. All in all, the elderly make up a very large portion of the "poor" and "near-poor" group in this country.
Why, then, does the Minister attack the elderly poor? On June 29, 1982 the Minister stated that measures in the budget, now contained in the Bill before us, "fully protect the lowest income Canadians and the working poor". Only those who are not in need will be asked to share in serious sacrifices which are required to bring our country out of the economic crisis, she said.
Is the Minister not by her own admission attacking those she purports to want to aid? How does she expect Members in this House or the people who are now receiving Old Age Security to take her seriously? Through the Bill before us, Bill C-131, the Minister of National Health and Welfare is attacking the very group which she has vowed will be protected.
Let me quote from a speech which the Minister made to the Men's Club of Vancouver in November, 1980. She said:
We have too many retired Canadians who find themselves living below or near the poverty line .. . Can you imagine if 53 per cent of the total population in Canada under age 65 had to rely on Government welfare payments to survive?
That would be shocking, shameful and economically disastrous. Why is it we ask this for our pensioners?
We say why indeed. What is the argument for bringing forth the proposals in this Bill? Supposedly to save an estimated $105 million a year, the Minister is cutting the already meagre welfare payments to the elderly poor. She does this by arguing that restraint is needed during the current recession.
The Liberal Government, of which this Minister is one of the key Ministers in its strategy for recovery, if there is one at all, is to put money in the hands of the rich for increased investment. Changes announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) in October, recommended to him by his blue ribbon committee on taxation, and changes which he will bring forward next week in his income tax Bill, will offer $750 million in tax breaks for the first year and $1.5 billion in the second year to Canada's wealthiest citizens.
How can the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who proclaims that she is the champion of justice in social programs in Canada, support such a policy? Where is her personal integrity? The Minister states that pension reform "is the highest social policy priority of the Government today".
I have tried in the years I have been here not to deal in personalities, but I have to say to the Minister, and 1 wish she were here, that we in the New Democratic Party, and I believe this would be true of old age pensioners, are bitterly disappointed in her. This Minister has frequently spoken about the needs of the old age citizens, the needs of the poor and the desirability and importance of maintaining our health care system, yet she is involved in cutting back on old age pensions and income security programs. We will see in the next year this Minister, through the federal Government and with the co-operation of the provincial Governments, cutting back on medical and hospital insurance.
We expected a great deal more from this Minister. In my opinion, if this Minister really believed what she has been preaching for the last couple of years, she would have resigned when the Government brought forward this kind of legislation.
This Bill will affect all those who now receive Old Age Security. That was 2.4 million people in 1981, of whom 57 per cent were women, many single or widowed. The argument has been advanced, and I say this in a cynical way, that in absolute terms the reductions in income as a result of the implementation of this Bill will be small. That is not true. It will seriously affect those who do not qualify for the Guaranteed Income Supplement and whose outside income does not provide them with adequate support.
Even a cursory examination of the facts reveals the weakness of the argument that the implementation of this Bill will affect only a relatively small amount of people. After all, prices are always relative to income. In a world of double-digit inflation, even the smallest cuts in income are debilitating for the elderly living in poverty.
More than 100,000 people will have the indexation of their pensions capped at 6 and 5 per cent, and suffer because they do not receive GIS. They are being told that they will not be
December 10, 1982

affected. However, the cost of living is still rising by 10 per cent. The Government's argument that by the summer of next year it will be down to 6 per cent is a specious argument. It will not happen. All the evidence is that the cost of living will be running at something like 9 per cent next summer. Those who have their old age pension increase capped at 6 per cent will have a reduction in their already too low standard of living of between 3 and 4 per cent.
We estimate that this Bill will cost those who depend on OAS $77 in 1983 and $220 in 1984, in total approximately $300 in the next 24 months. This is a piddling amount for this Liberal Government but a very significant amount for the 1.2 million Canadian senior citizens who depend on OAS to sustain themselves.
In the rush to apply six and five to all sectors of the economy, has the Government not forgotten its priorities and ignored the history of social welfare in Canada? While the Government will be niggardly with the incomes of those struggling to maintain their dignity and a decent standard of living in their old age, it has no compunction in allowing price increases well over their six and five guidelines for other sectors of the economy.
Let me give a few examples. In the summer of 1982, rent increases in Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation-owned housing projects in my Province were allowed of 16.4 per cent. The Ottawa-Alberta energy pricing agreement will increase the price of gasoline and home heating oil by 20 per cent or more for each of the next two years. In September, 1982 TransCanada PipeLines received, with the approval of the federal Cabinet, an increase of 16 per cent in natural gas transportation charges. That provides an average rate of return for the shareholders of 15.4 per cent. Shareholders can get 15.4 per cent, but old age pensioners will have their increases capped at six and five per cent.
In September of this year the excise tax on beer, wine, liquor and cigarettes was raised by 15 per cent by the federal Government. In October, 1982 the Government announced that unemployment premiums will go up by 39 per cent.
The Government overlooks the long-term effects of cutting indexation to six and five. This cuts the base on which further indexing will be calculated after 1984. That will be true only if we assume that the Government will go back to full indexing in 1984.
Once having breached the principle we have lived with for a number of years, that old age pensions and the Canada Pension would be increased quarterly by the amount that the cost of living goes up, having said that no matter how much the cost of living goes up the increase in indexation will be kept to six and five per cent, what assurance do the old age pensioners have that in 1984, given that we may still be in a recession, the Government will not say that it is going to continue to cap indexation? What assurance is there that any Government might not say that the economy is so bad and Government revenues so low that indexation could be done away with altogether? This is indeed a very serious step.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
I indicated earlier that we are discussing a reduction of $300 in the next two years in the amount that old age pensioners receive. If and when indexation begins at the full rate in 1984, the base on which the indexation will begin will be $300 less than it would have been. That means that all increases from then on will be based on a lower amount than they should have been. Therefore, what we are talking of concerning old age pensioners is not a reduction of $300 in their pensions. We are talking of a reduction in the life span of the old age pensioners because, after all, they will live 20 or more years after they begin to receive their pensions. We are talking of a reduction in real money to old age pensioners running into the hundreds of millions of dollars.
With the cut to 6 per cent in the increase in OAS in 1983, and generously assuming some reduction in the rate of inflation, there will be a reduction in real income of 5 per cent and more in future years for our pensioners. We have estimated that, realistically, the loss to the elderly in the next four years will not be $300, but rather $900.
The elderly are unjustly the victims of what has become a Government campaign of promising pension reform, as it did in the green paper tabled yesterday, while in fact it is eroding the fundamental basis of Canada's social security system. Old Age Security is one of the pillars of Canada's social security system. It represents 65 per cent of the income of the elderly from combined Old Age Security, Guaranteed Income Supplement, and the Canada Pension Plan or Quebec Pension Plan. From its inception in 1952 when the Old Age Security pension represented 17 per cent of the average industrial wage, the Old Age Security benefit has now been allowed to slip until it represents barely 13.5 per cent of the average industrial wage, amounting to a loss, in just a few years, of 20 per cent.
When the Old Age Security Program was enacted in 1951, after work done for many years in this House by Hon. Members of my Party, like the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre, by organizations such as the Canadian Welfare Council and the Canadian Labour Congress, it was a major achievement because we thought then that we had gone a long way toward abolishing the humiliation which had been part of the old pension system, the means test, which characterized the antiquated and limiting plans which preceded the open and universal program embodied in the Old Age Security Program.
In this Bill with which we are dealing today, the Government is asking the 2.4 million elderly Canadians to take a cut in benefits, but, further, it moves the whole social security program a few more paces back to the days when proud and dignified elderly citizens were required to submit to the means test. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because this Bill assumes that those who really need it can get the means tested Guaranteed Income Supplement. The Guaranteed Income Supplement has been excluded from the six and five limitations on the basis that it is more equitable to do so. This is part of the campaign which puts more and more emphasis on the means tested GIS as the basis for the whole system of social security.

December 10, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
The GIS was introduced in 1966 to assist pensioners with little or no income. However, OAS was to act as a bridge until the Canada Pension Plan had ripened sufficiently. In this Bill, the Government justifies cutting OAS by putting more weight on GIS to select a program.
We have fought for a long time so that universal old age pensions providing a decent living standard would be considered a right for all elderly Canadians, not a welfare program or not a gift. The fact is that people, particularly the elderly, will use a program much more when it is open to everyone. When a program is organized on a welfare basis, which we consider the GIS to be in part, requiring those who can participate to undergo a means test, it is clear that fewer will participate. The fact that over half of the 2.4 million Canadian pensioners are GIS recipients speaks for the Government's record on this issue. That fact alone demonstrates how many of our senior citizens are living in poverty. The latest statistics show that, of all individuals aged 65 years and over, almost 75 per cent have incomes under $10,000. The average income for this group is $9,280 a year. This includes Old Age Security benefits as well.
After the June budget, when the Bill was first announced the Minister of National Health and Welfare claimed that the budget "fully protects the lowest income Canadians and the working poor". She said that "only persons who are not in need will be asked to share in the serious sacrifices which are required to bring our country out of the economic crisis". I can only assume that the Minister, in presenting this piece of legislation, did not realize its full impact on the lives of elderly Canadians.
We say that the Government should withdraw the Bill. We expected a great deal more from the Minister. We say that if this country is in a recession, which it is, if sacrifices tnust be made, the sacrifices should be made by those people who can afford it, those people in the higher income brackets, those thousands of people who have incomes of $50,000 and $100,000 a year and pay no income tax at all because of the loopholes which are built into the income tax system as we have it.
Therefore, we say that if we must call on Canadians to make sacrifices, the last people upon whom we should call are retired Canadians who have contributed so much to building up the greatness of this country. They are the last people who should be called upon to make these sacrifices and, for that reason, we propose to vote against the bill.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Order, please. When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) had the floor.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my intervention on the subject of Bill C-131, an amendment to the Old Age Security Act, by mentioning my mother. She is a senior citizen, and I hope I am a dutiful son to her. Her means are modest as is the case with so many senior citizens today. I mention my mother not to garner sympathy or to make my speech different from any other, but only to underline the point that when we debate issues like this, so often it becomes "they".
Everything we do in this House really relates to people, both collectively and in a general sense. Not only do we have to think in terms of helping the most people most of the time, but in order to arrive at our decisions to do certain things in this House we have to remember that what we decide to do has an effect on individuals, because all of those broad "theys" are just a collection of individual people.
Somehow when we get into an extremely important subject such as this, it would seem that Members opposite suddenly garner the market on compassion and on understanding and really feel that we, the big bad Liberals and those that support the Government of the day, somehow have lost our mothers, our sons and our daughters. 1 submit that it takes a great deal of courage for a Government to introduce and support this kind of legislation, because if you take it out of context as one single act, yes, it becomes an unfair practice.
What we are really discussing in Bill C-131 is an amendment to the Old Age Security Act. We are saying that this is a necessary piece of legislation that is part of a broad range of programs designed to help all Canadians, and especially those senior citizens who have given so much to this country. What we are talking about is putting a cap on an increase. I do not think we should ever forget the fact that we are still talking, both in this piece of legislation and related pieces of legislation, about capping an increase. That is what is happening in this instance, but there is still further money to come.
In its wisdom the Government in this Bill has said to those of our citizens who are really going to be hurt the most: We understand your plight. We understand that this is their sole means of livelihood. We will do the best we can with limited funds and will maintain the status quo, and in fact do a little bit better for those people who are receiving the supplement. That is not the act of people who are not thinking, who lack compassion or understanding.
As always when we debate these points, one wonders about the information going around. I have heard all kinds of figures about what the actual dollar cost to the senior citizen might be. They range, from our side of the house, from $29 in 1983
December 10, 1982

and $52 in 1984 to figures conjured up on the other side which go as high as $900 over five or six years. 1 think we have to think about what is really being said. In effect, Hon. Members, without thinking, are saying, "We don't think that inflation will come down". That is what this is all about. The Hon. Member nods, "Yes, that's what we're saying". But may I just respectfully suggest to all of us in this House that if we, as Parliamentarians, do not believe that inflation will come down, do we not then fuel in our own way the expectations of Canadians of more inflation and not less? I might add, Mr. Speaker, that the trends of the moment indicate that in reality inflation is coming down. As inflation comes down, current projections show that in reality there may not even be a modest change in that capping of senior citizens' pensions, and they will at least maintain the level they are at now because inflation will hit that 6 per cent level.
Some very dear senior citizens 1 know have wondered why Members of Parliament, and other leaders in whatever part of society, do not concentrate more on encouraging businessmen to bring prices down. Then their dollar would be worth more and they would not be doing too badly. Senior citizens are saying, "You people in the labour movement, or in the work force in general, please consider, if you bring your expectations down just a little bit more, if you accept a little bit less, then we collectively as a nation gain and we won't have to get into this kind of legislation or greater controls somewhere down the line".
This Bill is a part of a package that no one is happy with, including my mother, but they recognize that it is part of a program which is trying to set an example whereby all of us can find a vehicle, if you will, in which to participate in a very important and necessary fight, and this is the fight to bring down inflation.
In this season of goodwill perhaps more Canadians should say, "Wait a minute. I think for a change I will truly think of my fellow man. Maybe I will be more careful in how I comment on the restraint of inflation. I will reconsider how 1 will gear my expectations for the future, how 1 will direct my thoughts toward wage increases, and so on, and 1 will consider that we collectively caused the problem and we can collectively solve the problem."
There is something else which the senior citizens of this country, and particularly my riding, recognize, Mr. Speaker, and that is that their sons, daughters and grandchildren have a right to expect something in the future. Many of the thoughtful senior citizens say, "We will, albeit it reluctantly, join in this fight against inflation. We will join in this fight to stabilize Canada not only for the sake of ourselves but for our children and grandchildren." 1 believe it is an accurate perception that senior citizens think of their children and grandchildren even more than we do in our sort of central sector of life. They want to make sure their grandchildren also have a place in the sun.
1 believe also we have to stop and think about introducing this kind of legislation from a political point of view. It is dynamite, because nothing can turn people on more, and no better Brownie points politically, in the crassest sense, can be
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
garnered, than when you start speaking of widows, orphans and children. But 1 believe that thoughtful Canadians recognize that no Government of any Party would introduce this kind of legislation unless it was being very thoughtful and responsible.
It is not an easy thing to do, nor is it easy to stand in my place today, Mr. Speaker, and support this kind of legislation.
I would not do it if I did not really believe that all of us collectively have to do something more to bring down inflation in order to make this a better country in which to live and to give all citizens a chance to participate more equally in its bounty. If this involves taking another look at programs, to be consistent, such as the Old Age Security Act and many others, then I say I do not want to do it; but I have done a lot of things in my life I did not want to do because it was the responsible thing to do, because it was necessary.
As I said on an earlier occasion, Mr. Speaker, I would really hate to think that all of these things will go for naught. We in this House have a larger responsibility than just getting elected the next time, or forming the Government the next time, and that is to keep this country on an even keel, to bring inflation down for the short term, the medium term and, what is even more important, the long term.
Hon. Members opposite have as much information as we on this side, or anyone else in the country, as to world-wide conditions in regards to productivity, what inflation rates are elsewhere, and what we have to do to compete in a world-wide situation because we belong on the same planet with these other countries. Members opposite know that. Therefore, they know this is not a trivial fight, this fight against inflation. It is an essential fight. We may be going to pull out of it now. People are uniting in a more meaningful way. We are beginning to move, all too slowly perhaps, but in a more positive direction. We have to accelerate that move and we also have to put ourselves in a position where we can say to the people of Canada, who also pay to help support our senior citizens whom we dearly love and are so proud of, that they will be in a position tomorrow to do even better. We can compete with anyone in the world, and we can do it well; but we cannot do this if Hon. Members opposite, I do not say deliberately, keep fueling these negative thoughts and expectations. If they keep saying day in and day out that there is no way inflation will come down, some sectors of the population will begin to believe they are right. And if they believe inflation is going to go up, maybe they would feel they should have a little bit more just in case, whereas in reality they should be saying collectively, "No, we don't like to take measures like this. We wish they weren't necessary but, by golly, it's a start."
If we all join in the fight collectively and sincerely, I think we can in fact bring down the inflation rate and can say to the senior citizens of this country, "We haven't been able to give you all you would like, or perhaps all we would like to give you, but you haven't lost ground because inflation did come down and your dollar is worth more". So that 6 per cent increase-it is an increase and I wish people would keep that in mind-is still realistic in these times.

December 10, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
So, Mr. Speaker, as I said at the beginning, I too have a mother. I am also just old enough to remember the Depression years. That has been brought into the debates of late a great deal as though only one side of the House knew anything about the Depression or about living in houses that were lit by kerosene lamps and all that sort of thing. I too have had my share of that and I have not forgotten; but 1 think I will be able to vote for this Bill, not because I want to see less in any way, at any time ever, go to our senior citizens, and not just because 1 want to see this as a positive step towards pension reform so we solve the ongoing problem of how we look after our people as they get older, but 1 will be able to vote with a clear conscience because I have thought it out and feel honestly that 1 have supported a measure which is absolutely necessary as part of a total package to bring down inflation, help restore confidence of Canadians and others in our country, so that we look after the immediate future and do the very large job of setting the stage for tomorrow.

Well, now I am smiling, Mr. Speaker, at the Hon. Member for Sarnia-Lambton. He was here ten years ago when his Government first admitted that inflation was out of control and indexing had to be brought in to protect the taxpayers, pensioners and all sorts of people against the ravages of inflation. Now they say, "Well, inflation is coming down anyway, so we do not need it". But here we have this legislation. Well, Mr. Speaker, that certainly is not the attitude we on this side of the House take when we look at a serious Bill like this one.
As I add a few words to the debate on Bill C-131, I have to ask myself why is this the last day of the debate? Why do we have this limited debate? The Government says it is an important Bill and it has to go through in a hurry, but we note the Government waited about four of five weeks from the date it was first introduced in the House until it was brought to the floor for debate. I suggest the reason is that the Government does not want the message to get out across the country. It is well known around here that short debates are not generally noticed across the country.

If we do not have a long, protracted debate, then the news is going to be on something else and people out there will not know what the debate was all about. I think the Parliamentary Secretary said there were 23 contributors to the debate, five from the Government side and obviously 18 from both Opposition Parties. We could ask why were there only five Liberals addressing the issues in this Bill. I suggest it was because the others were afraid-or ashamed, as the Hon. Member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) says. They were afraid to be seen to be eager to penalize pensioners.
Why were there so many speakers, relatively speaking, on this side? I am not admitting that 18 is a large number at all. Because people on this side know that the message has to get out and we have to have some kind of debate on a matter of deep principle which this debate involves. The House Leaders of both Parties on this side have said that we are opposed to this Bill, and what better way to show our opposition than to have a number of speakers get up and debate the issue and get the message out to the public.

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: OLD AGE SECURITY ACT (NO. 2) MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Smith) told us, with some pride I thought, that we had already had eight and a half hours of debate on this Bill and today we are probably going to get two or three more. Well, that is 11 hours. Now, is 1 1 hours too much? Would 21 hours or 31 hours be too much debate on a Bill which changes a very serious principle which was entrenched by this Parliament about ten years ago, that of indexing? We might also ask how many debating hours there has been between the time the Bill was introduced on October 28 and when the debate started, or even up until now.
I said this was an entrenched principle, Mr. Speaker, and to put that into perspective. I want to refer to the remarks of the
December 10, 1982

Prime Minister from just last year-not a decade ago, but just last year-at the National Pension Conference. I am quoting from his opening remarks:
Put simply, people must be protected in their retirement years. The Canadian Government has pledged that they will be better protected in the future than they are now. Pensions which are not protected against inflation naturally tend to dwindle over the years. People who thought they had purchased protection for the rest of their lives find that they have more serious financial problems the older they become.
That last sentence, of course, refers not to the old age pension but to contributory pensions. But the seniors of this country believe that they have contributed to the welfare and the coffers of this country and have purchased the protection promised to them by their Government. The Prime Minister went on in that same paragraph to say:
The unfairness of that situation ... is not tolerable in a nation which believes in social justice.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we have heard our Prime Minister tell us that the land is strong and we have heard him talk about the just society, and now we have heard what he said about pensioners. That was said 1981, it is now 1982, and what is he doing? Has he changed his principles? Has he changed his mind? I do not know. Now he is asking the pensioners of this country to take a cut in purchasing power-not in numbers of dollars but in purchasing power-which they can ill afford.
1 think we can go back to the original concept when indexing was entrenched in the legislation of this country and ask why we had indexing in the first place. The reason we had indexing was that inflation was found to be robbing seniors because of Government action. As Government action was robbing seniors of their purchasing power, the Government and Parliament thought they should take it upon themselves to restore that purchasing power. For nearly a decade, because the Government has seen fit to do nothing effective about the problem of inflation, we have had indexing in order to give seniors some measure of protection. It cannot be said that they are getting total protection from the ravages of inflation because of the way the consumer price index is calculated, which is not reflected in the living habits of all groups. Those on low income spend a greater proportion of that income on the necessities of life which are given a certain rating in the index.
We must consider who is going to suffer as a result of the proposition put forward today. Since the Guaranteed Income Supplement will be increased to cover the loss of the pension increase by those who receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement, I suppose we could say that only those with an income of over $8,912.40 will be affected. Let us round out that to $9,000. Every pensioner who has an income over $9,000 will have that income cut by about $3.40 in each of the first three months of 1983. That does not represent a lot of money to the Government but the increase to the pensioner will be cut from 11.5 to 6 per cent. That is quite a large percentage of the total pension income.
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
The Hon. Member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) and the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) both receive the old age pension and it will be cut. But they receive a salary as well, Mr. Speaker. There are thousands of pensioners with incomes of well over $9,000 who will not mind cutting back and giving up some pension. But that does not take away from the fact that it is a right and something that Parliament made a bargain on. It is something that Canadians should be able to rely on.
The Prime Minister talked about trust in one of his television speeches. How can he expect taxpayers and senior citizens to trust anyone here when the Government pulls tricks like this one?
Anyone who earns over $9,000 is not rich. Those who earn $10,000 will suffer more proportionately than the person whose income is $30,000. Should the cut come at $11,000? It is impossible to say. That is why the program should not have been adjusted the way the Government is trying to do it. It will make only a small dent in its huge deficit problem anyway.
I mentioned the $3 loss for the first three months of 1983 that will be incurred by pensioners on a cumulative basis. I have not figured out how much the total loss will be by the end of 1985 when indexing will be restored. That is not the whole problem, of course. The loss suffered by pensioners for those two years will carry on for the rest of their lives. The younger pensioners, those who can expect to live longer, will suffer more as the effects of the program accumulate.
I do not think many Members of the House would argue against the over-all restraint program. Six and five is good in certain ways. I think we must ask ourselves if the program is a good measure when it attacks the incomes of our senior citizens, those who can least protect themselves and the people who need to spend their money. The restraint program is good in so far as it will control Government expenditures and reduce Government deficits.
One of the things that we need in order to get the economy rolling again is to have more people investing and spending money. That helps to create jobs, to create multipliers and so on. It is well known that senior citizens, those with low incomes, spend it all. Every dollar the Government pulls out of the pension program will mean that one dollar less will circulate to improve the economy.
This Bill is a short-sighted action which may contribute a little bit to the solution of the Government's over-all problems. It is a niggardly action. It is directed at the wrong people in Canada. If it is successful in helping with the Government's program, then the seniors of Canada will not thank the government for it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I have not had a chance to listen to all the contributions to this debate on Bill C-131 but I have listened to the last two speakers.
I am pleased to take part in the debate this afternoon. This Bill gives us an opportunity not only to discuss the success of the Government's six and five program but it also gives us an

December 10, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
opportunity to show the good record of this Party in dealing with seniors over the last 30 years, if not more. In the brief time that I have been listening to speeches in the House, I have not heard too much about that, particularly from Members on the other side.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) says that he is in favour of the six and five program but that it should not affect certain types of people. Surely the whole success of the program is that it affects everybody on the federal payroll, those receiving federal pensions or federal allowances of one kind or another unless their incomes are below the poverty line. That is the psychological reason why the program has been a success-and it has been.
When the program was introduced in the June budget 1 wondered how it would be received in the country. 1 recall very well, as I am sure you do, Mr. Speaker, how the Opposition Parties ridiculed and pooh-poohed it following June 28, 1982, and how the provincial Premiers when they met in Halifax a month or so later also ridiculed and pooh-poohed it. Just a few months later Members on the other side like the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Quadra had to admit that it is a good program. A Gallup poll shows that two-thirds of the people in the country believe it is an excellent program and about the same proportion of union households agree with the need for it.
I was speaking to the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson) at lunch today and he said that the Chamber of Commerce in Summerside, Prince Edward Island had made a survey. The result showed that 90 per cent of those surveyed approved of the six and five program. Owners of large and small businesses are embracing the program with open arms. Some of the most influential names in the business world are actively promoting it as the only plan that will make our economy competitive again.
That is the name of the game. We cannot have double the inflation of the United States. We are a trading nation; our whole economy depends on our competitiveness in foreign markets. Unless we get our inflation rate down to near that of the United States, we cannot compete. Our manufacturers will not be capable of producing, new jobs will not be created and new investment will not take place. The more sensible and realistic Members of the Opposition realize that.
Some people say that while this is a good principle it should not affect this or that group-it should always affect some other group than the one they are dealing with at the present time.
As the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) mentioned, no Party is going to bring in legislation- particularly a Party that has been in power for most of the last 50 years-that is damaging to it unless it thinks there is a good reason for doing so.
In a few moments I will deal with our record in terms of senior citizens over the years, but particularly in the case of the Family Allowance legislation, Bill C-132, and Bill C-133, as far as it is concerned, unless we make all these groups subject to the six and five formula, with a bit of change in Bill
C-133 because of contributions, the psychology of the program will be badly affected.
We heard provincial Premiers and Members opposite deride the program in June and July, but let me look at what has happened since that time. Since then most Provinces have brought in their own programs. For example, in my Province of Ontario, Premier Davis brought in his own program after seeing how the wind was blowing in favour of six and five. After a few months he brought in his own 9 per cent and 5 per cent program, I believe it was. Most Premiers have done the same in one way or another.
I mentioned the business reaction before, and I mentioned that unless we get inflation down, our economy will not get rolling again and our people will not get back to work. It is worthwhile to mention the bases of finances here. At the present time, in December, 1982, people on OAS are receiving $246.92 per month. This time next year, December, 1983, they will be receiving an increase to $261.74 per month, and in December, 1984 they will be receiving $274.83 per month, another increase.
This will affect everyone on OAS, but what happens to the 53 per cent, more than half our seniors, who receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement at the present time? These 1.2 million seniors do not have any other real income. They receive the GIS or part of it. They will not be hurt at all by Bill C-131. Their GIS will be fully indexed in the coming two years. This new Bill will only be in effect until the end of 1984. In addition, those on GIS, more than half our seniors who need it most, will be compensated in lump sum payments for moneys they would otherwise lose by the OAS not being fully indexed for the next couple of years. Those who need it most among our seniors-and I am sure they are the ones about whom most of us are really concerned-will not be affected or hurt at all by this particular Bill.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra talked about the actual amount of money involved here. If we get inflation down to 6 per cent by the end of 1984, those receiving the OAS but not the GIS will lose about $29 in 1983 or less than $2.50 per month, and about $52 in 1984 or a bit more than $4 a month. For everybody, but particularly for our seniors, every dollar is important, but $2 or $4 per month is not the end of the world, if it helps get the idea firmly implanted in all parts of the country and with every group in the country that we are serious about the six and five program, that everybody should support it and do his or her part.
A few minutes ago 1 heard the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) refer to the fact that seniors are not only concerned about themselves, but they are concerned about their country, their families, their children and their grandchildren. They have gone through hard times themselves. They are the ones to whom we owe our comparative prosperity today. They are the ones who went through the wars and the Depression. They are the ones who worked hard to build the country after World War II. We owe an awful lot to those people.
December 10, 1982

In my area of Scarborough West there is a large proportion of senior citizens. This is what I tell them every time I see them, and this is what I believe. They are not only concerned about themselves; they are concerned about their grandchildren, many of whom do not have jobs. They are concerned because plants are closing down as a result of high inflation and lack of competitiveness in world markets. They are concerned that some of their children in middle age are unemployed for the first time. They are the ones who have always done their part. They answered the call to duty in the First and Second World Wars. Those are the ones who fought a hard fight during the Depression. They have always done their duty. People on OAS who have other income and do not receive the GIS want to do their part in the six and five campaign at the same time, which is a two-year campaign ending in 1984. 1 think Hon. Members will discover that as they go across the country.
There are some savings involved, but I do not think they are the big items in the Bill. After we take into account the money saved in reduced OAS increases and additional moneys paid out in GIS increases, we will have an estimated saving of $115 million. 1 suppose $115 million should not be sneezed at and 1 am not sneezing at it. Basically the idea is that this group of senior citizens who are above the poverty line and have other income want to do their part. It is true that many of them do not have too much other income. In some areas of the country seniors have a fair amount of other income, but not in my riding. If $100 million could be saved to contribute to employment opportunities elsewhere, they are willing to do their part.
What is our record? What is the record of the Liberal Party regarding senior citizens over the years? The Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson) who is in the Chair at present has been in the House for a long time and has participated in many debates. He will remember 1952 when the Hon. Louis St. Laurent brought in the first universal Old Age Security after discussions for a great number of years. Also he will remember that at that time it was effective at age 70. From 1966 to 1970 the age was reduced one year at a time to age 65. Then the Guaranteed Income Supplement came in for those seniors below the poverty line. Indexing came in for the first time in 1973. In 1975 the spouses' allowance came in for spouses between ages 60 and 64 who were living with spouses over age 65. Also, Mr. Speaker will remember that in 1979 the GIS was increased by another $20 flat rate as well as continuing to be indexed, and that in 1980 after the last election it was increased by another $30.

Yes, as my hon. friend says, this was all done by the Liberal Government.
Our record with respect to seniors does not just rest with Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Our Party brought in the Canada Pension Plan in the mid-1960s; it was the Government of the late Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson. That plan has been built up since 1966 and it is now becoming a more and more significant portion of pensions for workers once they retire. Perhaps just as important is our
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
record for seniors and everyone else with respect to Medicare and hospitalization.
My father was a lawyer. He was comparatively well off although he never thought so. He always had a fear, going through his life, that he would run into some dire medical disease or whatnot which would strip him of all his savings. My father was fairly well off, but this fear was always in the back of his mind.
Going back 20 years or so many people felt the same way. No matter how wealthy or poor they were a person's life savings could be wiped out if they suffered any kind of disease that required hospitalization. Hospitalization insurance came into being in the late 1950s. It was brought in by the Government of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. Medicare was introduced in 1964 or 1965 by the Government of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson. Senior citizens are more apt to have disease than younger people, but after hospitalization insurance and Medicare were brought in they no longer had this fear of having their life savings wiped out as a result of ill health.
We take hospitalization insurance and Medicare for granted in this country, but we should be reminded of the situation in the United States. Senator Kennedy and others have been fighting unsuccessfully for years trying to get the same sort of medicare legislation in the U.S. They have been fighting against medical lobbies of various kinds. There are some plans for those on charity, but other than that Americans have to pay high premiums to get some sort of health insurance. The Medicare and hospitalization schemes that we have here in Canada give very good protection. Medicare was brought in by my own Party and has played an important part in the over-all protection of senior citizens.
In closing, might I mention a program which I think delivers the most benefit per dollar to our seniors. I am, of course, referring to the New Horizons Program brought in by our Government. In my riding of Scarborough West, which comprises the old suburbs of East Toronto, we have many older people. This riding is not like other suburbs in the City. We have 20 to 25 senior citizens' clubs in this area. People who belong to these clubs are very active. They want to get involved. They not only live in senior citizens' towers but in family homes around the area as well. With a little bit of seed money, often no more than $5,000 per club for a year or two, they are able to get themselves organized. Some of them have weekly meetings. There are daily activities for some of them. These clubs are a focal point for sociability, athletic exercise and stimulating conversation for men and women. The New Horizons Program is an excellent program. I am sure Members on all sides of the House will agree with me that for a very few dollars we are able to get seniors to organize themselves, to take an interest in everything from nutrition to athletic endeavours. I also think of ceramics and woodworking. This is not a big program money-wise. It does not go into the

December 10, 1982
Old Age Security Act {No. 2)
billions as do some other programs for seniors that we have, but it is a very worth-while program.
I am not apologetic at all, nor is the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon and others on our side of the House who have spoken, for this piece of legislation. 1 can go into any seniors' group-I have 20-odd in my area-and say very clearly that they know who their friends have been over the last 30 years in this country. That is why we take the seats in Toronto, in the urban areas of the country and in Eastern Canada. These people know who their friends are. We do not come in making wild promises. We do not say, as do Members in the Party across from me here, sitting at the far end of the House from you, Mr. Speaker, that everything the Liberals do they will double automatically. We do not say that. Our seniors know who their friends are, and that is us.

speechtext:
I do think it would be stretching one's imagination to believe for one minute that the Hon. Member, or indeed any Member of the Liberal Party, could go into a senior citizens' home in Canada-other than some very wealthy ones-and expect to get out with any more than the clothes on their backs after they were through trying to explain this legislation. It is virtually unexplainable.
The Bill itself has been characterized in many, many ways over the course of this debate, but one of the best descriptions of the legislation is that it is a mean piece of legislation. It is designed, as it has to be designed if it is going to move in the area of restricting benefits, to impose a 6 per cent increase this year and a 5 per cent increase next year on old age pensions in terms of the Government's proposed plan to curb inflation. By the very nature and the very design of this Bill, it will curtail
old age pensioners' incomes. It has to. It cannot do anything else.
As I have said, the Bill limits the increase in old age pensions to a maximum of 6 per cent in 1983 and 5 per cent in 1984. As we all know, this pension previously had been fully indexed to the rate of inflation as measured to the consumer price index, which moves from time to time.
The legislation is basically directed against approximately 1.2 million senior citizens in this country who do not qualify for a full or partial Guaranteed Income Supplement. Looking at the scenario of a 10 per cent inflation rate, which will certainly occur this year, and also at the general economic situation, the scenario is bleaker now than it was some months ago, first because the American economy has not responded in the way that President Reagan and the powers that be in the United States hoped for, and, second, because we are on the verge of a very detrimental trade war. This will slow down the rate of recovery as well.
Everyone is hoping for a recovery. Everyone is hoping that consumer confidence will pick up and people will start to buy goods and services once again. If that does not happen, and it is increasingly more evident that it will not, then we could see, even with the six and five program, that inflation will remain at very substantial levels, well above the hoped for targets of six and five.
If we were to take an inflation rate of approximately 10 per cent, which is what it is presently, each of the 1.2 million old age pensioners would lose $290 in the next two years. On a year to year basis, that would be approximately $70 in 1983 and $220 in 1984. Those who will be affected to the greatest degree will be the single elderly with incomes slightly above the $8,900 or, to round it off, $9,000 which is the cut-off figure for those who receive the full Guaranteed Income Supplement. Anyone with an income marginally above that will certainly be affected very significantly. Those with incomes marginally above the $9,000 level will be the hardest hit. They are the ones who cannot afford a decrease.
Those who earn $8,900 a year receive a little less than $25 a day. The Government is going to carry out its fight against inflation by telling them that they have to sacrifice. The sacrifice made by someone who receives $25 a day is significantly more than the sacrifice made by someone who earns significantly more. Those who can least afford to make a contribution in the fight against inflation are being asked to make biggest contribution.
An elderly married couple with an income of just over $15,000 per year will lose approximately $580 over the next two years. Clearly the Government intends to fight inflation on the backs of the elderly, admittedly not all but 1.2 million of them, which is a significant number. The cut-off level will be $9,000 for a single person and $15,000 for a married couple. Those marginally above that cut-off level will have to do further belt-tightening at a time when 1 suspect the belt is drawn as tightly as it can be.
December 10, 1982

How much does the Government expect to save with this proposal? If the savings amounted to millions and millions of dollars and if one were hard hearted enough, one could say that it would be worth it in view of the good to the Canadian economy. However, that is not the case. I do not know what the savings will be, but I am sure they will be small in comparison to the total amount of money that this Government should be trying to save.
The sum will be small compared to the detailed criticisms made this past week by the Auditor General, particularly with regard to Crown corporations. The savings will be minuscule when compared to total Government spending. We are not talking about a lot of money, but we are talking about a significant amount of misery. That is an area we must look at.
A country is not judged on how it treats its more privileged citizens, but how it treats those at the lower levels, the low income earners. It can be judged in no other way. We are judged by the compassion we have for those less fortunate than ourselves. That is how we judge our friends, neighbours and, in fact, other countries.
If someone were to look at Canada, they would see that the Government is asking this Parliament to pass legislation which asks those who are already struggling to struggle even harder. We would not be judged in a very positive way.
Closure is being imposed and this afternoon we will vote on this Bill. We should hang our heads in shame for what we are doing to a significant portion of our population who helped to make this country what it is today, a good place to live.
The elderly in our society scrimped, saved and sacrifices in order that we might have what is ours today. Today we will be saying to these people that they must scrimp, save and cut back on their standard of living even more. That is not right, and the Members of my Party will not support it. While we agree generally that inflation must be dealt with, we cannot in good conscience vote for a measure like this in the same week that the Auditor General came out with horror stories of excess Government spending in the hundreds of millions of dollars over the past year by this Government, which is now asking us to impose a further hardship on our old age pensioners. It is not right, it is not fair, it should be voted against and it should be condemned by every sane person in this country.
