Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate because there are some people who need to be reminded of what has occurred. It has been said that a country is judged by the way it treats its senior citizens. It is equally true that a Party can be judged in the same way. Given that circumstance, I think the Liberals can stand tall. What Hon. Members should recall, particularly those in the Opposition, is the fact that the GIS and the Old Age Security will not be reduced to the 6 and 5 per cent for those who are on GIS and Old Age Security. We will have full indexing in that particular area.
The senior citizens of this country will not judge the Liberals or this particular Government on one measure alone. They
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
will look at the over-all picture of how they have been treated by a particular Government. I think the Opposition should be remained of the fact, because its Members, of course, never mention it, that something like $8.5 billion is paid directly to Canadian senior citizens on an annual basis through the Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and the spouses' allowances. That amounts to $8.5 billion, approximately one-tenth to one-twelfth of the total expenditures of the federal Government, including transfer payments, moneys that we must pay out in interest on the national debt, and money that we spend on the Department of National Defence, be they direct or be they transfer payments.
Senior citizens, those over the age of 65, have gone through two world wars and a Depression as well as the conflict in Korea. They know what it is to plan and to prepare, but, more important, they know what it is to be independent, and they like to have the accompanying feeling of pride. Therefore, I was particularly proud to have been elected in 1968 when one of the earlier moves of the Government was to bring in low rental housing for senior citizens. The mood and the approach of the Canadian public has changed quite a bit. In my day there was the sort of thought that grandparents in their old age would probably live with one of their children. That is not the case nowadays. The time came when people felt that senior citizens lost a bit of their dignity. They were quite often shut off in one room. Sometimes they had to put up with grandchildren whom they were frankly ill-equipped to look after on a permanent basis. They had spent a quarter of a lifetime looking after children and felt that they were entitled to something just a little bit better.
Low rental housing units for senior citizens gives them that sense of independence and the opportunity to invite friends and relatives over. They are still able to visit their grandchildren so that they can enjoy them, and when the children start becoming a little less than congenial, they can be dumped back on their parents' laps and looked after in this way. This gives senior citizens the sense of independence, value and worth and, primarily the opportunity of feeling that they are in a position in which they can act as they have acted all their lives, namely, in the position where they are not beholden to anyone.
Bringing in the Old Age Security so that everyone receives the benefits on a universal basis is appropriate, not so much for people who really do not need it but for the average working person who puts aside a few dollars so that he or she will have something upon which to retire, supplemented by the old age pension. These people are encouraged to save because they will then have their pensions or savings looked after and the old age pension as well, and that is across the board.
Others, through no fault of their own, are not in a position to put a few dollars aside because they have not received sufficient compensation for their work to permit them to do so. Some senior citizens incurred heavy medical expenses before

December 10, 1982
Old Age Security Act (No. 2)
the introduction of Medicare. 1 say, thank heaven for Medicare. Many senior citizens lost their life savings because of a sickness in the family. These savings could have been wiped out in a six month period. Senior citizens no longer have the fear that if they go to the doctor it will eat into their incomes. The Liberal Government has brought in the kind of legislation to allay such fears.
Who stands to gain the most if we are able, through this program, to bring down the rate of inflation? Obviously, it will be the people on fixed incomes and, very obviously, those who are drawing only old age pensions and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Inflation is invidious. It cuts right across the board. I believe the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) indicated earlier that people who had set aside money for their pensions had seen it being eaten away by inflation. Therefore, we have indexed pensions so that they will not be eaten away in this manner.
No one is suggesting that the old age pension should be decreased in its value and in payments to pensioners, and no one is suggesting that, for all time, indexing should be taken away. However, if this program is successful, then our civil servants who are under the six and five program and the senior citizens who are finding their pensions increasing by 6 per cent and 5 per cent rather than according to the consumer price index, are the ones who will have taken the leadership role, once again, in aiding the economy. They will be the chief beneficiaries when the inflation rate comes down to an appropriate level.
Obviously, the Government cannot do it all alone. With the success of the six and five program, many people in the private sector are now coming forward and saying, "We actually initiated that ourselves. We had put freezes on our salaries, on the salaries of members of boards of directors and midmanagement, and in some instances we had actually cut salaries or the amount of compensation payable to our employees and, in some cases, even encouraged employees to take early retirement at wages similar to those they would have received if they had stayed on". In that way they tried to rationalize the situation so that their employees would be able to meet the difficulties lying ahead.
The six and five program is appropriate because it will help our senior citizens. They will probably become the chief beneficiaries. My colleague-my colleagues-

Mr. Speaker, I would just like, in discussing Bill C-131 today, to draw to the attention of the Members opposite who have spoken that it was not only by the votes of the Liberal Government Members that these senior citizens programs were put in place. They were supported by all Parties in this House. There was some discussion and some debate on each occasion as to whether it was the right step, or there was enough money, or the allocation was proper or a certain group would be left out. But all Parties in this House, when all the measures that had been discussed earlier were voted on, supported those measures.
Let us take a look at the basic provisions in Bill C-131. It amends the Old Age Security Act, and the purpose for this legislation is the implementation of the six and five. This is what we are told. This is what speaker after speaker on the Government side reiterated, that this legislation is necessary to bring forth the Government's restraint program known as six and five.
In specific terms, the Old Age Security payment that is now fixed at $246.92 per month will be increased by 6 per cent in 1983 and by a further five per cent in 1984. The result is that the absolute limit of that increase, the only increase that can take place by the end of 1983, will be $14.82 per monthly payment, bringing it to $261.74, slightly more than $3,000 for the full year, and you can compare it: $2,999.04 versus $3,140.88.
Why is this action being taken in the guise of restraint? The answer is quite simple, it is being done in this way so as to save $90 million in 1983 and $150 million in 1984. The Government is now saying that the senior citizens, the people who built this country, will have to be restrained. The total funds that we are talking about over the two years, $240 million, will be taken from 1.1. million Canadians, and $125 million will be paid to 1.2 million Canadians. Those are the Canadians who receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement. So we are only talking in this House right now about $110 million. This is restraint? It is not restraint, it is re-allocation.
I do not think that Members on the Goverment side are being quite straightforward with people receiving Old Age Security. It is not restraint, it is re-allocation. Why is it necessary to re-allocate funds in that manner? We have been told that we have to bring inflation down, below six and five, and we say that that is an admirable goal. The problem arises that while the oldest people of this country, the senior citizens, are being asked-not really asked, it is being demanded of them-to take part of this program, the Government itself is not taking part. The Government is going on its merry way continuing to spend, continuing to increase. I think we all know of much less harmful instances to the fabric of this country on which the Government could practise restraint than the senior citizens who have helped to build this country.
It takes away the encouragement, the feeling of self-sufficiency that most people in this country have, as they feel it is their responsibility to provide in their senior years. We come to a point where a very small segment of society will be affected by this Bill, but those people are proud that they have been

If we look at the situation of corporations, we have heard the New Democratic Party say we should tax corporations more heavily. I think it was the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) who said the other day that is where we can get the money, tax the corporations, because the corporations are making excessive profits. Corporate profits in the last year have fallen 50 per cent. They are 50 per cent lower. It is not a matter of increasing by only six and five; it is a matter of actually declining absolutely by 50 per cent from where they had been the year before. And as a result of that decline, people are being thrown out of work, firms are shutting their doors, and that is increasing the burden on individuals, and it is increasing the burden on the state which has to pay unemployment insurance and other forms of social assistance to those who have lost their jobs.
I believe, rightfully so, the corporate sector, the business sector, has to pay their fair share, but is that the sector which can absorb more of-the load right now? I suggest to you at this point in time that that sector cannot carry more of a burden than it is already carrying. As far as public servants themselves are concerned, the working population of public servants has been subjected to the six and five program. Their salaries will go up by 6 per cent this year and 5 per cent next year.
We have heard a great deal of discussion in committee with regards to Bill C-133 and some of the other legislation, that indeed it is not fair to apply restraint to pensions in the various areas, the general transfer programs, because where it is fair to apply it to wages and salaries, it is not fair to apply it to pensions. The reason is that those who are working are able, through collective bargaining and other means, once the restraint is over, to recapture that lost ground, and this is not possible for pensioners. That gave me pause for thought for a long time because it sounds right. It sounds right to say yes, pensioners cannot bargain, they cannot get an increase, and workers can because there is such a thing as bargaining.
Then I went back and looked at the facts to see if it was true. If you look at the figures and the facts you will find that, indeed, workers are not able to extract more from the system than the system is able to pay. Workers' salaries and wages have not increased out of line with productivity over the long term. They have not increased at astronomical rates above inflation over the long term. Certainly, in short-term periods that has been the case, where wages in a particular sector have gone up. But you would expect that. If there is a shortage of certain kinds of workers, their wages will go up. But over the five to ten-year period wages on average have gone up about the same as inflation, plus a productivity factor.

It is not, therefore, fair to say that workers are able to recapture what they might have lost during a period of restraint. Capital Punishment

subsubtopic: NATIONAL REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by complimenting the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) for bringing this motion calling for a national referendum to be held on the subject of capital punishment.
1 take pleasure in this debate largely because the motion is so similar to the one that I introduced in the House in November, 1976. At that time I called for a national referendum to be held on the same subject. 1 very clearly recall the debate, which happened to be on November 15, of that year. I remember what the Hon. Members on the Liberal benches were saying in the argument against my motion.
The Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville, now the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), who was a reputed constitutional expert on the subject, entered the debate. He had two very singular arguments for putting down my motion. One was that such a referendum would be very divisive to the country. He called upon history and the conscription debate of the 1940s when in fact a referendum was very divisive. The way the question was put, the experience was very divisive for the country. 1 accept that particular argument on that particular subject for that particular period of time.
The other argument which he put to the House at that time was that a referendum would be considered unconstitutional, that in fact it was against British parliamentary tradition to have a referendum because the elected Members of Parliament have been chosen by the population at large to represent them in Ottawa in this case, to speak on behalf of the people and therefore it was not the tradition of the British parliamentary system to hold referenda.
It was very interesting to follow that debate. As I said, it went on during the day of November 15. While we were debating that motion in this House, the good citizens of the Province of Quebec were going to the polls. On the evening of November 15 we watched the results come in. They had elected a Pequiste Government.
You never saw such a marvelous conversion in the Liberal ranks on the subject of referenda. What had been an anathema to the country before, a divisive subject, a divisive mechanism, an unconstitutional mechanism, overnight gained immediate credibility.
I recall that within a year of that debate the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduced Bill C-9 in this Chamber. It was to provide the mechanism whereby in this British parliamentary system, which is not designed to allow for referenda to be held, all of a sudden after a particular dramatic election in the Province of Quebec there would be a mechanism, and it was articulated by the Prime Minsiter of Canada. A Bill was tabled in this House which would provide and legitimize the mechanism whereby a referendum could be held on that subject.
The Bill which the Prime Minister tabled in the House at that time had a very narrow reference. It was made to deal with one particular topic. If in that very narrow reference there could be a mechanism and legitimacy provided for a referendum in this country, why could it not be applied to subjects other than the matter of separatism? If it is legitimate to have a referendum to cover that very important subject to the future of our nation, why not on the matter of capital punishment?
If there is one subject which all Members of the House are consistently confronted with in their constituencies, across the board, why is it not possible to have a referendum on the subject of capital punishment? That is a question that comes to all Members whether they are abolitionists or in favour of capital punishment.
There was a very simple reason for that. Public opinion polls consistently show that between 70 and 80 per cent of the population is in favour of capital punishment. This is very clearly understood by all Members of Parliament, and indeed all candidates in every general election. Ail Members of Parliament accept that by far the majority of Canadian people are in support of capital punishment.
The fact that in 1976 the Parliament of Canada voted against the wishes of the Canadian people has been one of the singular features of our Parliament which has tightened the level of cynicism in our country toward the work of Members of Parliament. If on the one hand the people of Canada are saying this is what we want you to do and they make that known to Members of Parliament during an election campaign and through representations later, and in the face of that known position the Parliament of Canada votes against the wishes of the majority of the Canadian people, that in itself is enough to heighten the level of cynicism toward the political process in our country.
In 1976 we were promised that there would be a free vote. Some free vote. I remember that free vote and the pressure that there was on Government Members to vote with the Government on that issue. It is because the Parliament of Canada has not fulfilled the wishes of the Canadian people that we have this continual request for a referendum on the subject of capital punishment. It is because of this continual request that the Hon. Member for Erie has fulfilled the request of his constituents that we present to the House this motion, which is a further request that the Government honour the wishes of the majority of the Canadian people.
On every other issue, the Government always makes the argument that they are doing something because that is what the people of Canada want them to do. It does not matter whether it is the subject of PetroCan, six and five or any other subject, the rationale on the part of the Government is that the people of Canada want it to do it.
December 10, 1982

If the people of Canada want the Government to do that, and the argument of the Government is that it wants to do what the people of Canada want it to do, then why does it not do it on this subject? Very clearly, the answer is that the Government thinks that the people of Canada are wrong. I think that one of the most cherished rights we have in this country, above every other right, is the right to be wrong. It was our right. That is what brings about the differences of opinion in our country. That is what makes democracy a vital experience in our country, because one side thinks the other side is wrong, and that is all right. If the people of Canada, 70 per cent to 80 per cent, are wrong, it is their right to be wrong, and it is the requirement of the Parliament of Canada to fulfil the wishes of the Canadian people, even if it thinks the Canadian people are wrong.
It seems to me that when we go through an election campaign, one of the frequent campaign statements by all candidates and one which we have all said here in one way or another is, "Let me represent you in Ottawa. I want to represent you in Ottawa". That is a good statement to make to the electorate. However, on this subject, when the people of Canada said, "I want you to represent me in Ottawa," the majority of the Members of Parliament said, "No, I will not do that. I will represent myself, not the majority of the Canadian people". Candidates in a campaign never say, "When I go to Ottawa, I will think for myself, and even if you want me to do something else, I will do what I want to do because I happen to think that I am right". Candidates are always saying, "I want to represent you." They never say, "When you elect me, I will go to Ottawa and I will study the issues but I will do exactly as 1 please".

speechtext: "Or as I am told".

subsubtopic: NATIONAL REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Yes, or, as the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) says, "Or as I am told." That is a fact. It seems to me that if people want to be elected on a popular or populist basis, and be honest with the electorate when they become elected, saying, "I want to represent you", then they must represent the Canadian people on every issue.
I pay tribute to my predecessor in the riding of Surrey-White Rock-North Delta. He happened to be a Member of the New Democratic Party. However, he was an honourable man. He took a poll of Surrey-White Rock-North Delta residents at that time and found that something like 80 per cent of the people of that riding wanted him to vote for capital punishment. He was the only Member of that caucus to vote in favour of capital punishment because he was determined to do what his constituents wanted him to do. I tip my hat to him because he maintained his sense of honour.
If there is one thing that we cannot afford in this country, it is a spirit of elitism on the part of the elected representatives who say to the electorate, "I can do as 1 please". We cannot
Capital Punishment
afford that kind of elitism. If we want to be a populist Parliament, if we want to represent the people of Canada, we must represent what they want, whether or not we agree with it. Frankly, I think one of the most anguishing votes in which I ever participated was one in which I disagreed and 1 voted against what I thought was good for the country because I thought the people wanted me to vote that way, and it was on the Constitution. I do not think that the Constitution that we passed in this Chamber is a good Constitution. However, I know that the people of Canada, by far, wanted us to get it over with, wanted to have it done with, and they wanted a Charter of Rights and Freedoms, whether they agreed with that particular Charter or not, and I voted for it, much to my dismay, worry and conviction that in the long run it would not be good for the country.
There is one argument I want to put forward with regard to the issue of capital punishment itself and, with that, I will turn the floor over to some other Hon. Member. I spoke on this subject on June 8, 1976, I believe, and the former Solicitor General, who was piloting that Bill through the House, is sitting opposite me here today. I know that he hung on every word I said during that debate. The one point I want to make is that those people who want to see the abolition of capital punishment continuously say that a civilized nation cannot put people to death. Civilization depends on two very important factors. The first is that it be an orderly society and the second is that it be a compassionate society. That is a civilized society.
Murderers, particularly those who kill prison guards and policemen, are the most anarchistic, order-destroying people in our country. To protect those people who want to create anarchy in families, in communities and in nations is a contradiction of the word "civilization", because they are anarchists. Why should we protect those people whose personal goal is to create anarchy?
The second point I want to make with regard to civilization is that it is a hallmark of all civilizations, if, indeed, they are comprised of civilized people, that they will protect the unguarded and the weak from those who would ravish them. They will protect those who have suffered the consequences of the actions of murderers and rapists and they will protect those who have suffered as a result of that kind of ravishment and provide some kind of support mechanism afterwards.
I want to ask you, Mr. Speaker, of all the hours of time we have spent in this Chamber discussing the rights of criminals who have taken the lives of other people, how much time have we spent thinking about the anguish of those people who are members of the families of those who have been murdered?

Is that the hallmark of a civilized society, to devote all of its attention to those who rape and pillage and kill, and ignore the anguish of those who are ravaged?
It is because of our distorted values, our distorted goals and our distorted laws that I commend the Member for Erie for bringing forward this motion that will let the people of Canada express their will on the subject of capital punishment.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am also pleased to participate in this debate on what I consider to be a very important and serious question, one that deserves much more time than we can give it today.
Let me respond right away to the last remarks of the Hon. Member. 1 am not speaking here today for the Government, but he criticized the Government for spending too much time on the issue of capital punishment and the abolition of capital punishment, and not on what we should do for victims and so on.
If that is the case, why is he today supporting a motion or a Bill which would bring about a reconsideration of capital punishment? Why did he not bring forward today a Bill or motion which would allow us to deal with the subject of the victims of crime.
The point of my speech, which 1 will get to in due course, is that our time would have have been much better spent today if we considered motions and Bills that, first, dealt with the causes of crime and how to prevent crime; second, how we can help the victims of crime, and the Hon. Member seems to be in favour of that; and, third, how we can have better rehabilitation programs in prison so that when people leave prison they will go to a productive life and not back into a life of crime.
I will return to those in a minute, but I see many contradictions in the Hon. Member's speech. If he is really interested in those things, why should we have a referendum on capital punishment?
I am not dogmatically opposed to referenda on some matters but I do not think that a referendum or a plebiscite is the best way to settle or solve a complex emotional question in this country. Certainly it is not the best way to decide on the important issue of capital punishment.
December 10, 1982

In the British parliamentary system, which is part of our Constitution, it is not that it is unconstitutional to have referenda or plebiscites, but it is against the general spirit of our system. 1 think in all Canadian history, at the federal level, we have had two plebiscites, not referenda 1 make the distinction. Generally a referendum is when we allow all voters to vote, but the result of that vote becomes law without any further action by Parliament or town councils or legislatures. On the other hand, we have had plebiscites in the past 100 years of our history on two occasions, for conscription and with respect to our drinking laws. These were plebiscites. Once the vote was taken the Government still had to deal with the issue in Parliament. As you know, in the conscription plebiscite, the Government took action not quite in line with the plebiscite results because it felt it would have very badly divided the country. Also around the turn of the century, the same was done with the plebiscite on alcohol.
In Britain, the only time that 1 can recall that a plebiscite or referendum was taken was on the case of joining the Common Market, and again it was a plebiscite and not a binding referendum.
The fact that it is not normal in the British parliamentary system does not mean that it cannot be used. I maintain very strongly that it is the wrong way to deal with complex emotional issues.
During his speech the Hon. Member opposite referred to public opinion polls. He said public opinion polls have shown over and over again that the public in Canada favours capital punishment. 1 would ask this House, are we saying that we are favour of public opinion polls as a basis of governing this country?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

subsubtopic: NATIONAL REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: That is not the way Governments under the British parliamentary system have governed for over 600 years, and it is not the way they should govern. I would agree with the Hon. Member that too often today some Governments are attempting to govern by polls.

It is completely contrary to the traditions of the British parliamentary system to govern by public opinion polls.

With respect to this very complex and very emotional issue, it would seem to me that if we were to decide this issue by referendum, which is one of life and death-we are dealing here with the lives of individuals-the whole question would carry with it more emotion than light and reason.
Another argument that 1 give against having referenda or plebiscites settle this very important question is that much will depend on how you formulate the question. It is obvious that if you put out a public opinion poll or a plebiscite or a referendum in a community or in a country where there has been a problem of murder, where there have been some severe and horrible murders and the people are upset, and rightly so, they should be upset at horrible murders, but if you put out an opinion poll or a plebiscite in those communities immediately afterwards and asked, are you in favour or against capital punishment as the penalty for murder, of course they are going to say, yes. You are putting before a group of people who are upset by murders being committed in their community one solution to deal with the problem of murder, and asking them whether or not they agree.
I say how you put the question is very important. I have seen public opinion polls on this issue where instead of merely putting forward one solution to the problem of murder, the pollster put forward ten solutions. He says, we have a serious problem of murder in this country-this was back in the sixties-and here are some solutions: stricter gun laws, better community education programs for youth, better programs for alcoholics and drug abusers, and so on. He listed ten things and asked, would you put these in the priority in which you think they are most important in dealing with the problem of murder. In that type of poll, capital punishment came fourth or fifth, not at the top. Even then it was subject to emotional problems and lack of information and so on. I submit very strongly that this would be the wrong way to deal with this very complex and important issue.
The Hon. Member says that many of us changed our views on referenda when the Parti Quebecois put the question of independence on a referendum in the Province of Quebec. I am a Member from the Province of Quebec. I am a citizen of Quebec. 1 never approved of that referendum as a way of settling that question. I thought it was completely wrong. I thought it was a way in which to appeal to the emotions and not to the reasons of the people of the Province. I would have much preferred that the whole question be dealt with within the National Assembly of Quebec and within the Parliament of this country, not by a referendum, and I stand by that today. Once we had the referendum, of course, we had to deal with it, and we fought hard on the "no" side of the question and we won, but it was not our preferred way of dealing with that question, not mine, in any case, as a citizen of Quebec.

1 would like to comment on the Hon. Member's remarks with respect to the free vote which we had in 1976 on this issue. He questioned whether it was a free vote or not. I would like to tell him, since I was the Minister who introduced the Bill and had to pilot it through this Parliament, that as far as 1 was concerned, it was a free vote. I was on this side and I had a hang of a time getting the support I needed to get that Bill through. I recall the day I stood up in the House and answered the question and said, "yes, it will be a free vote for everyone except the Cabinet", because I thought if the Cabinet approved of the Bill, certainly it would not be a free vote for them. 1 was contradicted at the time by the House Leader and the Prime Minister who said it would be a free vote for everyone. In fact, we only won that vote by six votes, I believe, on the final reading of the Bill, and by 15 votes on the second reading. It was a very close vote. Thirty per cent of the Government caucus voted against the Bill. 1 believe, on the other side, 30 per cent of their caucus voted for the abolition, and almost the entire New Democratic Party voted for the Bill, and all the Social Credit Party voted against. But they should have been involved, Mr. Speaker, in the problems which I had on this side of the House when I had the Official Whip, the Whip of my own Party, going around trying to convince people to vote for retention". Despite the fact that several Members of this House voted against the Bill to abolish capital punishment, several of them were taken into the Cabinet afterwards, and one is our new President of the Liberal Party, Iona Campagnola, who voted against me on that issue as a backbencher. It was not held against her. No pressure was brought to bear. She was still brought into the Cabinet as an important and productive Member of our Caucus.

I do not agree with what happened to him yesterday, but that is a different issue. I believe very strongly in consulting with my constituents and with the public of Canada. That is essential in our system. We consult, we go to public meetings, we listen to the population, but we listen to their arguments, we do not simply count heads. That is not our system of Government. We are elected to office on platforms with a political Party and we are expected to study questions in depth, to look at the pros and cons of a question, and in good conscience make a decision for the public good in Canada. We are not expected merely to count heads, which is suggested by this resolution. You go out and listen to the arguments, you debate. 1 have done that on many occasions in this country. And it was difficult to go into packed meetings where the people came with blood in their eye, and so on, because there
had been a horrible murder in their community. It was right they were angry. I agree with them. I am angry myself when I hear of these awful murders. But you listen to the argument. Reason should prevail in our Government and not numbers.
What is suggested to me by the type of motion that is introduced today, what always is conveyed to me, is the so-called trial of Christ, where Pilate had Christ before him and it was his responsibility to make the decision for Christ, and the mob was shouting, "crucify Him. Crucify Him." So Pilate washed his hands and allowed Christ to be dealt with as the mob wanted and not in accordance with justice as he, who was responsible for Roman justice in that colony, should have done. That is what plebiscites, referenda and public opinion polls always suggest to me. It is mob rule and not rule by rationale and reason.
I would like to submit very strongly that there is no basis for reconsidering capital punishment at this time. Since the abolition of capital punishment, the murder rate in this country has steadily declined, not because capital punishment was abolished, but because lots of other things have happened. In 1975 there were 701 murders in Canada. In 1976, the year we abolished capital punishment, there were 668 murders. In 1977, there were 710 murders. This was a gradual increase, but in 1978 there were 658 murders. In 1979 there were 631 murders. In 1980 there were 593 murders. We have not received the final statistics for last year, but they declined again. Therefore, there has been a decline every year.

subsubtopic: NATIONAL REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: How about the attempted murders?

subsubtopic: NATIONAL REFERENDUM ON CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
I do not know what the number of attempted murders was before the abolition. That is a red herring, Mr. Speaker. Let them make their speeches, if they can, and I admit that the time is too limited today. We have no statistics on the attempted murders either before abolition or after abolition. The point I am making is that I can recall the debate very well. Members who were against the abolition said, "If you abolish capital punishment murderers will run amuck in the streets and the murder rate will go out of control." In fact it has not. The murder rate has gone down, thank God. Consequently, what we should be considering today is the question which the Hon. Member raised: how can we more effectively reduce the rate of murder in this country? What are the preventive measures which we can introduce to deal with murder? The issue is not what the penalty should be after a person is murdered, if we catch the criminal and find him guilty. The issue is: what should we do to prevent that murder in the first place; better policing, better rehabilitation, more effective alcohol control, drug control programs, better community recreation programs, and better housing in communities where crime is bred more rapidly than other communities. These are the things we should be concentrating on.
December 10, 1982

We should also be concentrating on how we should help the victims of crime. The Member was right when he discussed that issue. I agree with him 100 per cent. These are the kinds of things we should be discussing, how to better compensate the victims of crime, how to give them crisis centres, because a lot of murders are committed in families where women are battered by their husbands, along with their children. We should provide more assistance for that sort of situation. We should give better training to our social workers to take people out of crisis situations.
In addition, in accordance with the motion I put to the House on December 8, 1982. I believe the Government should set up an independent review group to examine the present 25-year minimum before eligibility for parole on first degree murder, and we should be looking at its impact on prisons and prison populations. And I believe such a review group should recommend new, more flexible provisions which will protect the public to the greatest extent possible, but at the same time provide a greater opportunity for rehabilitation for those serving sentences in prison.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that we should concentrate on the causes of murder and not the penalty, family support, urban environment, education, treatment of emotional disorders, alcohol, drugs, health care, community involvement, gun control, police training, pro-active policing, effective corrections programs, and so on. And there must be more concern, assistance, support and better compensation for the victims of crime, especially victims of violent crime. It is not just the criminal who is responsible for these crimes but, to

a certain extent, all of us. Society is responsible because we fail every time there is violence in our society. I think most of us would admit that the supreme value in our society is human life. And if the supreme value is human life, then the organized state should never repeat the act of the criminal. A criminal justice system, based on revenge, is not appropriate to a civilized society. We must look for solutions that are humane and civilized, but also effective and ones which offer security to the population.
